catalog_quote: 2.12. Stress and Length. Amoss 1961:4-5 discusses Nooksack stress. As she points out, raised relative pitch and increased vowel length are features of primary stress and raised relative pitch with no increased vowel length are features of secondary stress. ... She also notes that monosyllabic words regularly get primary stress when spoken in isolation. ... Amoss also reports (1961:15) that ŚS̀ is the most common stress pattern, ŚS is less common, S...Ś is also possible, S̀Ś also occurs, and Ś₁Ś₂ can occur when S₂ is a stressed suffix (S = syllable here). My findings confirm most of Amoss's conclusions but differ in a few places. Neither I nor LT or BE found secondary stress to be common. It has the qualities mentioned but is rare and not distinctive (phonemic) at the word level. In the cases where it occurs in citation forms it is analyzable as optionally present or absent (for example in the environments _SŚ and ŚS(S)_). I did not find it myself in ŚS̀ or ŚS̀S̀ or S̀Ś in the words quoted in Amoss 1961 nor in any others, although it may occur in rare cases. So at word level [ˋ] is predictable and non-phonemic in the speech of GS, SJ and LG. At sentence level [ˋ] is more frequent (even in sentences of only two words), but it is an allophone of /´/, occurring in normal and rapid speech in free variation with [´] on monosyllables adjacent to words with /´/.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is phonemic (listed in the phoneme inventory) and its position is not given by a rule: the commonest pattern is stress on the first of two syllables (ŚS̀ / ŚS), but second-syllable and final stress (S̀Ś, S..Ś) also occur, some suffixes are inherently stressed and keep their stress even beside a stressed root (double primary stress allowed), and monosyllables always carry primary stress in isolation. Secondary stress is rare and non-phonemic at word level.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress (raised pitch without added length) exists but Galloway, L. Thompson and B. Efrat found it rare; it is predictable and non-phonemic at the word level, optionally present in environments _SŚ and ŚS(S)_, and more frequent at sentence level as an allophone of /´/ on monosyllables adjacent to stressed words.
new_statements.exceptions: Halkomelem-influenced speakers (LG, EF) occasionally use high-falling pitch on long primary-stressed vowels (pp. 116-117); multiple primary stress is allowed (stressed suffix + stressed reduplication, Galloway 1984 ICSNL19 p. 91); durative reduplication shifts stress to the last vowel (ibid. p. 89); the imperative suffix -lə is usually unstressed (Galloway 1997:201); George Swanaset's extra final stress when sounding words out is an artifact (Galloway 2012).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms, three speakers (GS = George Swanaset, SJ = Sindick Jimmy, LG = Louisa George). Galloway lists stress /´/ as a phoneme in the inventory (p. 86) and treats secondary stress [ˋ] as predictable/non-phonemic at word level and an allophone of /´/ at sentence level. Sentence-level stress reductions are noted as predictable (Galloway 1997:201). Patterns are reported as frequencies (from Amoss 1961:15), not as a rule; no source opened gives an explicit placement rule for polysyllables.
new_statements.identity_note: Nooksack proper (nook1247), data from the last fluent/partial speakers George Swanaset, Sindick Jimmy, Louisa George and Esther Fidele; Galloway notes Upriver Halkomelem influence (incl. occasional high-falling pitch on stressed long vowels) in the speech of GS, LG and EF. No dialect split at issue.

sources.note: Sec. 1 Phonemic Inventory (p. 86) lists 'Stress ´' as a phoneme. Sec. 2.12 'Stress and Length' (pp. 115-116): primary stress = raised pitch + lengthening (about 1/2 mora), secondary = raised pitch without length; monosyllables get primary stress in isolation; citing Amoss 1961:15, ŚS̀ is the most common pattern, ŚS less common, S..Ś possible, S̀Ś occurs, Ś₁Ś₂ when S₂ is a stressed suffix; Galloway finds secondary stress rare and non-phonemic at word level (an allophone of /´/ at sentence level); Halkomelem-influenced speakers sometimes use high-falling pitch on long stressed vowels.

sources.note: 'When a word has only one vowel in Nooksack it gets primary stress so in the phonemic orthography stress does not need to be written on this word'; Fetzer's double stress on some words is an artifact of George Swanaset sounding words out syllable by syllable with extra final stress, which other speakers (Sindick Jimmy, Louisa George) did not do.

sources.note: pp. 200-201: 'Length is not phonemic in Nooksack; stressed vowels automatically receive length of from one to one-half mora (Amoss 1961, Galloway 1983a)'; 'few words in Nooksack are normally without phonemic stress'; sentence-level stress reductions are predictable and citation forms restore phonemic stress; the strong-imperative suffix -lə is usually unstressed.
Only: 'An acute accent (´) is placed on the accented syllable'; cites Galloway 1984 and Richardson & Galloway 2011; no placement rule.
